chunks: "I go around the schematic and ask each part two questions: what does it dissipate, and what does it do to ripple.
The input capacitor carries the pulsed input current: RMS about I out square root of D(1-D) , so its ESR loss is small but its ESR and ESL set the input ripple and the spike on the switch-loop.
The high-side FET has conduction loss D I to the 2R DS(on) and the biggest switching loss, because it turns on and off against the full voltage.
The low-side FET conducts for (1-D) so it has the largest conduction loss, plus dead-time and reverse-recovery losses.
The driver and controller add gate-drive loss, Q gVf , and quiescent current, which matter at light load.
The inductor loses power in its winding resistance, I squared times DCR , and in its core, and its value sets the ripple current.
The output capacitor barely affects efficiency, because the ripple current through its ESR is small, but it sets the output ripple through C and ESR. In a 12 volts to 3.
3 volts, 2 amps, 500 kilohertz example that works out to about 460 milliwatts of loss: the low-side FET about 180, the high-side about 140, the inductor about 120, and everything else small.
So efficiency is about 93. 5%, and the output ripple, about 17 millivolts, comes from the inductor and output capacitor, not from the FETs.
The design tension is that making the FETs lower-resistance makes them bigger with more gate charge, making L bigger lowers ripple but raises DCR and slows the transient."
